questions.text: In a two-period model, a consumer is a borrower in period 1 when what holds?

options.a: Second-period consumption equals second-period income.
options.c: The interest rate is zero.
options.d: First-period consumption is below first-period income.

questions.text: In the two-period model, a consumer is a lender in period 1 when what holds?

options.a: First-period consumption is greater than first-period income.
options.b: First-period consumption is less than first-period income.
options.c: Future consumption exceeds current consumption.
options.d: Second-period income must be zero.

questions.text: What is the slope of the intertemporal budget line when period-1 consumption is on the horizontal axis?
What happens to the budget line's slope in absolute value when the interest rate rises?

options.a: It increases.
options.c: It decreases.
options.d: It becomes zero.

questions.text: How can a two-period budget constraint be expressed in present-value terms?
How can a two-period budget constraint be expressed in future-value terms?
At a zero interest rate, how much is €1 next period worth today?

options.a: An amount determined by borrowing behavior alone.

questions.text: For a positive interest rate r, the present value of €1 received one period later is what?

options.a: 1/(1+r) euros.
options.c: (1+r) euros.
options.d: (1-r) squared euros.

questions.text: What is the period-1 consumption intercept of the two-period budget line?
What is the period-2 consumption intercept of the two-period budget line?
Why does the intertemporal budget line pass through the endowment bundle?

options.a: The endowment is necessarily the midpoint of the line.
options.c: Interest income always equals future income.
options.d: Consuming exactly the income of each period requires neither borrowing nor lending.

questions.text: When the interest rate changes and period incomes remain fixed, what happens to the budget line?

options.a: It shifts in parallel toward the origin.
options.c: It pivots around the endowment bundle.
options.d: It pivots around the origin, not the endowment.

questions.text: What does the model assume about the interest rate for borrowing and lending?

options.a: There is no ability to transfer consumption across periods.
options.b: Borrowing is free and lending is prohibited.
options.c: Both activities are possible at the same constant rate r.
options.d: Borrowing is always at twice the lending rate.

questions.text: What does a consumer choose at an interior optimum under standard preferences?

options.a: A point where current and future income are exactly equal.
options.b: A point with a budget-line slope of zero.
options.c: A point where the intertemporal marginal rate of substitution matches 1+r in absolute value.
options.d: The maximum possible future consumption regardless of preferences.

questions.text: A lender faces a rise in the interest rate. Which change is unambiguously true in the slide's model?

options.a: The consumer must switch to borrowing.
options.c: The consumer cannot optimally switch to being a borrower if initially a lender.
options.d: Future consumption must fall.

questions.text: Why can a higher interest rate benefit someone who remains a lender?

options.a: Saved resources earn a higher return in period 2.
options.c: The budget line ceases to bind.
options.d: Borrowing becomes cheaper.

questions.text: For a borrower who remains a borrower when the interest rate rises, welfare does what?

options.a: Becomes independent of preferences.
options.c: Rises without exception.
options.d: Remains exactly unchanged.

questions.text: Why is the response of saving to a higher interest rate generally ambiguous?

options.a: Only production technology determines savings.
options.c: A higher rate never changes the budget slope.
options.d: Substitution and income effects can push first-period consumption in opposite directions.

questions.text: For a lender, which is the substitution incentive created by a higher interest rate?

options.a: Shift consumption toward period 1, because saving returns less.
options.b: Consume strictly equal amounts in each period.
options.c: Consume only the endowment in both periods.
options.d: Shift consumption toward period 2, as future consumption becomes cheaper relative to current consumption.

questions.text: For a borrower, the substitution effect of a higher interest rate encourages what?

options.a: Less current consumption relative to future consumption.
options.b: No response because borrowers cannot save.
options.c: More borrowing at an unchanged cost.
options.d: More current consumption relative to future consumption.

questions.text: What makes the income effect of an interest-rate rise different for borrowers and lenders?

options.a: A lender gains purchasing power, while a borrower loses purchasing power.
options.c: Both gain purchasing power equally.
options.d: Borrower and lender status has no relation to wealth changes.

questions.text: If a consumer starts at the endowment bundle, how does an interest-rate change affect the feasibility of that bundle?

options.a: It becomes feasible only if the consumer borrows.
options.b: It becomes feasible only if income is constant across periods.
options.c: It remains feasible because no intertemporal trade is required.
options.d: It becomes infeasible for all higher rates.

questions.text: What does present value allow economists to compare?

options.a: Payments received at different dates in common current-value units.
options.b: Preferences of consumers without knowing their income.
options.c: Profits without knowing prices.
options.d: Marginal utilities without a utility function.

questions.text: Why is a future payment discounted at positive interest rates?

options.a: Future money is always riskier by assumption.
options.b: Money available today could earn interest before that future date.
options.c: Every consumer is a borrower.
options.d: The price of consumption must rise each period.

questions.text: What is the present value of a payment A received two periods from today at fixed rate r?

options.a: A/(1-r)^2 for all r.

questions.text: As the positive interest rate increases, the present value of a fixed future payment does what?

options.a: Decreases.
options.c: Remains unchanged.
options.d: First decreases and then always becomes negative.

questions.text: As the payment date moves further into the future, its present value at a positive constant rate does what?

options.a: Rises.
options.c: Remains fixed.
options.d: Falls.

questions.text: When evaluating mutually exclusive investments with comparable risk and cost, which decision rule is appropriate?

options.a: Prefer the investment with the highest undiscounted sum of future revenues.
options.b: Prefer the one with the largest nominal payment at the end.
options.c: Prefer the investment with the highest net present value.
options.d: Prefer the investment with the longest payment delay.

questions.text: What is the net present value rule for accepting a standalone investment?

options.a: Accept if the first cash flow is negative.
options.b: Accept if NPV is positive, assuming the market interest rate is the relevant discount rate.
options.c: Accept if total undiscounted revenue is positive, irrespective of costs.
options.d: Accept only if NPV is exactly zero.

questions.text: Why might an investment paying more money in the future be inferior to one paying less now?

options.a: Its discounted present value may be smaller.
options.b: Future money must have lower nominal value.
options.c: It must have a negative accounting profit.
options.d: Earlier cash flows are always risk-free and later cash flows are always worthless.

questions.text: Suppose a project costs €100 now and pays €110 in one year. What is its NPV at 10% interest?
If two income streams have equal present value and the consumer can borrow and lend freely at r, what is true?

options.a: They yield the same affordable set of consumption plans.
options.b: The stream with higher future income always dominates.
options.c: The stream with higher first-period income always makes the consumer better off.
options.d: One stream must lead to borrowing and the other to lending.

questions.text: If one income endowment has strictly higher present value than another, what follows under frictionless credit markets?

options.a: It has a lower period-1 intercept.
options.b: Its owner must save in period 1.
options.c: Its owner must prefer future consumption.
options.d: It offers a larger intertemporal consumption opportunity set.

questions.text: For a three-period model with a constant r, how is period-3 consumption discounted to period 1?

options.a: By dividing by (1+r) only.
options.c: It is not discounted at all.
options.d: By dividing by (1+r)^2.

questions.text: What is the economic interpretation of choosing to lend in period 1?

options.a: Increasing current consumption without reducing future resources.
options.b: Forgoing current consumption to finance greater future consumption.
options.c: Choosing an endowment with lower present value.
options.d: Consuming future income before it is earned.

questions.text: Which feature determines whether a given consumer borrows or lends, assuming a competitive capital market?

options.a: Only second-period income.
options.b: The interest rate alone regardless of income and preferences.
options.c: The consumer's preferences relative to their endowment and the intertemporal price ratio.
options.d: Only the nominal amount of first-period income.

questions.text: Why is the present-value budget formulation especially useful?

options.a: It forces consumption to equal income separately in each period.
options.b: It eliminates the need to specify an interest rate.
options.c: It expresses resources and spending at different dates in a common unit.
options.d: It assumes that consumers cannot save.

questions.text: If the market interest rate is positive, which of the following is true for a payment of €100 received next year?

options.a: Its present value is exactly €100.
options.c: Its present value is zero.
options.d: Its present value is below €100.

questions.text: What does the slope of the illustrated intertemporal budget line represent?

options.a: The price of period-2 consumption divided by total income.
options.c: The ratio of the two incomes, -m1/m2.
options.d: The negative discount factor, -1/(1+r).
